disregard

/diss-rih-GARD/ - the stress falls on GARD · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Disregard means to see something and choose to pay it no attention — to ignore it on purpose.

Astronomers disregard the first night of data from a new telescope, letting the instrument settle before trusting a single reading.

Example

The label on the epoxy said twenty-four hours of clamp time; the boatwright, forty years at his bench, decided he knew better and disregarded it, unclamping the repair at dusk to make the morning tide. Halfway down the coast, the joint let go. He had read the instruction — read it and set it aside, which is the whole shape of the word.

Disregard is the exact word because it requires seeing first: you must notice a thing before you can pay it no further attention. To overlook the label would be an accident; to disobey it outright would make a point of the refusal. Disregarding is quieter than that and more willful than a miss — attention withdrawn on purpose.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

neglect: To neglect something is to fail to give it the care it is owed — often over a long stretch, and often without ever deciding to. Disregard is a single, deliberate act: you see the instruction and set it aside. Neglect names a duty dropped; disregard names a choice made.

snub: To snub is to pointedly ignore a person — and to mean the person to see it, since the cold shoulder is the message. Disregard is quieter and usually aims at things: a warning, a memo, a rule seen and then set aside without ceremony.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

heed: to give careful attention to

obey: to do as an instruction says

Where it sits · how knowingly it is brushed aside — overlook → disregard → disobey

overlook vs. disregard: To overlook a rule is to miss it — no choice involved; to disregard it is to read it and put it out of mind.

disobey vs. disregard: Disobey goes further than disregard: the clerk who disregards a memo just works as if it never came, while the one who disobeys it does the opposite of what it says and stands ready to answer for it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: not

Root — regard

Root — regard: to look at, to watch

Put it together

Put it together: Dis- (not) + regard (to look at, to watch, from Old French regarder) = to not-look. Regard is literally watching — holding something in your gaze — and disregard un-watches it: the eyes, and the attention behind them, are turned away on purpose.

Use the root in a new word: regard

Use the root in a new word: regard: The harbor pilots held the old lighthouse keeper in high regard long after the lamp was automated.

Word Choice

neutral

Disregard is the act of ignoring — attention deliberately withheld — and it can even be innocent or wise: astronomers disregard a telescope's first night, and pilots disregard a gauge the tower has confirmed faulty. Its unit-mate dismissive adds attitude: to disregard a report is simply not to act on it, while a dismissive reception tells the author to her face that it wasn't worth reading.
